title: OCIH 12 — Test
src: Jaw Movements & Functions of the TMJ

mcqs.q: Rotational movement of the TMJ occurs in which compartment?
mcqs.explain: Rotation occurs in the lower (meniscomandibular) compartment; gliding occurs in the upper (meniscotemporal) compartment.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the basic jaw movements?
mcqs.explain: The jaw movements are protrusion, retraction, elevation, depression and lateral; the skull itself does not rotate at the TMJ.

mcqs.q: When the mouth opens, the FIRST 20–25 mm of movement is:
mcqs.explain: Opening is biphasic: rotational (hinge) for the first 20–25 mm, then translational (gliding) for wider opening.

mcqs.q: At the end of wide mouth opening, the condyle comes to lie under the:
mcqs.explain: During wide opening, hinge movement is followed by gliding, and the head/condyle comes to lie under the articular tubercle (eminence).

mcqs.q: During protrusion (protraction) of the mandible:
opts: The articular disc glides forward over the upper surface and the condyle moves with it
mcqs.explain: In protraction the disc glides forward over the upper articular surface and the condyle moves with it; the reverse is retraction.

mcqs.q: During chewing, if the RIGHT condyle slides forward while the left only rotates, the chin shifts:
mcqs.explain: When one condyle slides forward and the other rotates in place, the chin shifts toward the non-sliding side; alternating produces the grinding motion.

mcqs.q: Which muscle is the MAIN protrusive muscle of the mandible?
mcqs.explain: The lateral pterygoid is the main protrusive muscle; its lower head also depresses (opens) the mandible.

mcqs.q: Which muscle spans the zygomatic arch to the angle of the mandible and is a powerful elevator?
mcqs.explain: The masseter runs from the zygomatic arch to the angle of the mandible; it is a powerful elevator (chewing) muscle.

mcqs.q: Which muscle elevates the mandible, with posterior fibres aiding retraction?
mcqs.explain: The temporalis (origin temporal fossa, insertion coronoid process) elevates the mandible; its posterior fibres retract and it aids grinding.

mcqs.q: The LOWER head of the lateral pterygoid produces:
mcqs.explain: The upper head of lateral pterygoid assists elevation, while the lower head produces depression (opening).

mcqs.q: Which are the SECONDARY (accessory) muscles of mastication?
mcqs.explain: The suprahyoid group (digastric, mylohyoid, geniohyoid) act as secondary/depressor muscles.

mcqs.q: Lateral (side-to-side) movement is mainly produced by:
mcqs.explain: Lateral movement is mainly produced by the contralateral pterygoids, controlled by the ipsilateral temporalis and masseter and restricted by ligaments.

mcqs.q: Which is a function of the TMJ?
opts: Mastication, speech, swallowing and maintaining rest position/airway
mcqs.explain: TMJ functions include mastication, speech (phonation), swallowing, maintaining rest posture/airway, stress absorption and coordinating both joints for occlusion.

mcqs.q: Shock absorption during heavy biting is provided by the:
mcqs.explain: The articular disc and synovial fluid help absorb shock and distribute force during heavy biting.

mcqs.q: On TMJ examination, a grating sound from rough articular surfaces is called:
mcqs.explain: Crepitus is a grating sound (often from degenerative surfaces); clicking is a sharp single sound. Both are noted on examination.

mcqs.q: The distance measured between the incisal edges on maximal opening is the:
mcqs.explain: The interincisal (maximal opening) distance is measured with a ruler or Vernier callipers as part of TMJ examination.

mcqs.q: In condylar hyperplasia, the chin typically:
opts: Deviates to the unaffected (opposite) side, with a posterior open bite on the affected side
mcqs.explain: Condylar hyperplasia (enlarged condyle) deviates the chin to the unaffected side and causes a posterior open bite on the affected side ('inverted L' neck).

mcqs.q: Condylar hypoplasia is:
opts: Failure of the condyle to reach normal size (small condyle and fossa)
mcqs.explain: Condylar hypoplasia is failure of the condyle to attain normal size; the condyle and fossa are proportionally small.

mcqs.q: A bifid condyle is characterised radiographically by:
opts: A notch/cleft giving a heart shape on the AP view
mcqs.explain: A bifid condyle has a vertical depression/notch in the centre of the condylar head, giving a heart shape on the anteroposterior view; it is usually an incidental, asymptomatic finding.

mcqs.q: The medial pterygoid muscle has:
opts: Two heads (superficial and deep) and elevates/grinds the mandible
A single head that depresses the mandible
mcqs.explain: The medial pterygoid has superficial (maxillary tuberosity) and deep (lateral pterygoid plate/palatine) heads, inserting at the angle of the mandible; it elevates and grinds.

mcqs.q: Closing the mouth (elevation) reverses the opening sequence, ending with:
mcqs.explain: Closing reverses opening: the gliding (translational) phase reverses first, then the hinge (rotational) phase.

mcqs.q: Which muscle's posterior fibres assist in RETRACTION of the mandible?
mcqs.explain: The posterior fibres of the temporalis assist retraction of the mandible.

mcqs.q: The two joint compartments during normal function:
opts: Have different roles — upper for gliding, lower for rotation
mcqs.explain: The upper (meniscotemporal) compartment performs gliding/translation and the lower (meniscomandibular) compartment performs rotation/hinge.

mcqs.q: Over-movement of the jaw is prevented by:
mcqs.explain: Excessive movement is restricted by the ligaments and joint surfaces, while muscles control the direction of movement.

saqs.q: Describe the biphasic opening movement of the TMJ.
saqs.a: Opening is rotational (hinge) for the first 20–25 mm (lower compartment), then translational (gliding) (upper compartment) for wider opening; the condyle ends under the articular eminence. Closing reverses it.

saqs.q: Explain how chewing (lateral) movement is produced.
saqs.a: By alternating side-to-side movements: one condyle slides forward while the other rotates in place, shifting the chin to the non-sliding side; alternating gives the grinding motion.

saqs.q: Name the four primary muscles of mastication and their main actions.
List the functions of the TMJ.
saqs.a: Mastication (hinge + glide), speech, swallowing, maintaining rest position/airway, stress absorption (disc/synovial fluid), and coordination of both joints for occlusion.
Inspection (swelling/symmetry/clicking), palpation (pre-/intra-auricular, tenderness, crepitus), auscultation; assess range of movement and the interincisal distance.

saqs.q: Describe condylar hyperplasia and its clinical signs.
saqs.a: A developmental enlargement of the condylar head; the chin deviates to the unaffected side, with a posterior open bite on the affected side and an elongated 'inverted L' condylar neck.

saqs.q: Contrast condylar hypoplasia and a bifid condyle.
saqs.a: Hypoplasia: condyle fails to reach normal size (small condyle/fossa). Bifid condyle: a central notch/cleft giving a heart shape on AP view (usually asymptomatic).
